subtitle: 'Polars 2.0 made the streaming engine the default. Order-dependent queries that were stable in 1.x now change from run to run, and one argument fixes them.'
summary: 'Polars 2.0 runs lazy queries on the streaming engine by default, and the streaming engine does not guarantee row order. Running five order-dependent queries 20 times each on the same file, Polars 1.44.2 matched the explicit-order answer every time, while Polars 2.0.0 and 2.1.0 got four of the five wrong on every run, with a different answer each time and only a handful of customers affected. Keeping order in the join, or sorting inside the expression, fixed every run. Switching back to the in-memory engine did not fully restore the old answers, and DuckDB in R behaves the same way without an ORDER BY.'

knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      # NOT the default `*_files/figure-html/`. The ignoreFiles
                      # setting in config.toml drops `_files$`, so images written
                      # there never reach the published site.
                      fig.path = "figs/")
pct <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
fmt <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)

Polars 2.0 shipped on 6 October, and its headline change is that `collect()` on a lazy query now
runs on the streaming engine. The [announcement](https://pola.rs/posts/announcing-polars-2/) gives
row order as one reason that needed a major version, and the
[upgrade guide](https://docs.pola.rs/releases/upgrade/2/) is clear that the streaming engine does
not guarantee row order for joins, group-bys, and similar operations. What it cannot tell you is
what that does to code written when order happened to hold. So I ran the same queries, with
default settings, under Polars 1.44.2 (the last 1.x release) and 2.1.0 (the current release, out
on 25 October). 2.0.0 gave the same results in every run I made before 2.1.0 shipped.

```{r data, include=FALSE}
library(arrow)
set.seed(20261030)
n_cust <- 100000L
n_ev <- 2000000L
customers <- data.frame(customer_id = 0:(n_cust - 1L),
                        segment = sample(c("a", "b", "c", "d"), n_cust, TRUE))
# An event log in time order, so event_id is also the order of purchases
events <- data.frame(event_id = 0:(n_ev - 1L),
                     customer_id = sort(sample.int(n_cust, n_ev, TRUE) - 1L),
                     amount = round(rgamma(n_ev, shape = 2, scale = 20), 2))
events_path <- file.path(tempdir(), "events.parquet")
customers_path <- file.path(tempdir(), "customers.parquet")
write_parquet(events, events_path)
write_parquet(customers, customers_path)
```

```{python audit, file="audit.py", include=FALSE}
```

```{python run2, include=FALSE}
res2 = audit(r.events_path, r.customers_path, runs=20)
```

```{r run1, include=FALSE}
# The same script under the last 1.x release, in its own interpreter
py1 <- Sys.getenv("POLARS1_PYTHON")
stopifnot(nzchar(py1), file.exists(py1))
# -B: write no __pycache__ into the post folder, which Hugo would publish
res1 <- jsonlite::fromJSON(system2(py1, c("-B", "run_audit.py", shQuote(events_path),
                                          shQuote(customers_path), "20"), stdout = TRUE))
res2 <- reticulate::py$res2
stopifnot(res1$polars == "1.44.2", res2$polars == "2.1.0")
q <- names(res2$queries)
tab <- data.frame(
  query = q,
  v1 = vapply(q, function(k) res1$queries[[k]]$runs_wrong, 1L),
  v2 = vapply(q, function(k) res2$queries[[k]]$runs_wrong, 1L),
  distinct2 = vapply(q, function(k) res2$queries[[k]]$distinct, 1L),
  row.names = NULL)
n_broken <- sum(tab$v2 > 0)
# The front matter quotes these, so a change in the results must stop the render
stopifnot(all(tab$v1 == 0), n_broken == 4, all(tab$v2[tab$v2 > 0] == 20))
```

```{r table, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(tab, col.names = c("Query", "1.44.2: runs wrong of 20",
                                "2.1.0: runs wrong of 20", "2.1.0: distinct answers"),
             align = "lrrr")
```

Under 1.44.2 every query matched its explicit-order version on every run. Under 2.1.0,
`r n_broken` of the 5 were wrong on `r if (all(tab$v2[tab$v2 > 0] == 20)) "every one of the 20 runs" else "some runs"`,
and for those `r n_broken` no two runs agreed with each other. The code did not change. Only the
version did.

The data are two tables written to Parquet from R: `r fmt(n_ev)` purchases in time order and
`r fmt(n_cust)` customers.

```{r data-show, ref.label="data", eval=FALSE}
```

The audit joins them, runs five queries whose answer depends on row order, and compares each
run with the same query written so the order is explicit. The same file runs under both
versions.

```{python audit-show, file="audit.py", eval=FALSE}
```

```{python run2-show, ref.label="run2", eval=FALSE}
```

## How much is wrong

```{python size}
ev, cu = pl.scan_parquet(r.events_path), pl.scan_parquet(r.customers_path)
truth = {k: q.collect(engine="in-memory")
         for k, q in queries(ev, cu, explicit=True).items()}
first_wrong, total_rows, total_err, index_wrong = [], [], [], []
for _ in range(10):
    got = {k: q.collect() for k, q in queries(ev, cu, explicit=False).items()}
    a = got["first purchase per customer"]["amount"]
    first_wrong.append(int((a != truth["first purchase per customer"]["amount"]).sum()))
    d = (got["running total per customer"]["running"]
         - truth["running total per customer"]["running"]).abs()
    total_rows.append(int((d > 1e-6).sum()))
    total_err.append(float(d.max()))
    picked = set(got["row index, first 1,000"]["event_id"].to_list())
    index_wrong.append(1000 - len(picked & set(truth["row index, first 1,000"]["event_id"].to_list())))
```

```{r size-r, include=FALSE}
fw <- unlist(reticulate::py$first_wrong)
tr <- unlist(reticulate::py$total_rows)
te <- unlist(reticulate::py$total_err)
iw <- unlist(reticulate::py$index_wrong)
```

Not much, which is the problem. Across 10 runs, the first purchase came back wrong for
between `r min(fw)` and `r max(fw)` of the `r fmt(n_cust)` customers. A share that small passes
every eyeball check. The running totals were wrong on between `r fmt(min(tr))` and
`r fmt(max(tr))` of the `r fmt(n_ev)` rows, but a wrong one was off by as much as
`r fmt(round(max(te)))`, in a column where the median purchase is `r round(median(events$amount))`. The row index was the loud failure: of the first 1,000 rows,
between `r fmt(min(iw))` and `r fmt(max(iw))` were different rows from the ones 1.44.2 picked.

A small test fixture does not hide it. The same first-purchase query on synthetic logs of
different sizes, 10 runs each:

```{python scale}
import numpy as np

def first_purchase_errors(n_events, runs=10, seed=1):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    n_c = max(n_events // 20, 10)
    c = pl.LazyFrame({"customer_id": np.arange(n_c)})
    e = pl.LazyFrame({"event_id": np.arange(n_events),
                      "customer_id": np.sort(rng.integers(0, n_c, n_events)),
                      "amount": rng.gamma(2.0, 20.0, n_events).round(2)})
    q = queries(e, c, explicit=False)["first purchase per customer"]
    ref = queries(e, c, explicit=True)["first purchase per customer"].collect(engine="in-memory")
    return n_c, [int((q.collect()["amount"] != ref["amount"]).sum()) for _ in range(runs)]

scale = {}
for n in [1_000, 10_000, 100_000, 1_000_000, 10_000_000]:
    n_c, bad = first_purchase_errors(n)
    scale[n] = [n_c, min(bad), max(bad), sum(b > 0 for b in bad)]
    print(f"{n:>10,} events  {n_c:>7,} customers  wrong in {scale[n][3]:>2}/10 runs, "
          f"{min(bad)} to {max(bad)} customers")
```

```{r scale-r, include=FALSE}
sc <- lapply(reticulate::py$scale, unlist)
s1 <- sc[["1000"]]
s10 <- sc[["10000000"]]
```

On a thousand rows the error reaches up to `r pct(s1[3] / s1[1])` of the customers, so a test that
compares output with a stored answer `r if (s1[4] == 10) "fails on every run" else paste("fails on", s1[4], "of 10 runs")`.
On ten million rows it is `r s10[2]` to `r s10[3]` customers out of `r fmt(s10[1])`.

## Why it happens

The streaming engine splits the data into chunks and works on them in parallel. Operations that
do not need order, such as a join, may hand chunks on in whatever order they finish. `first()`,
`cum_sum()`, `unique(keep="first")`, and `with_row_index()` all read the order they are given, so
they inherit the shuffle. `head(20)` came through intact here, but nothing promises that it will.

None of this is a bug. A Polars issue opened in November 2024 set out that
[left-join order should not be guaranteed](https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/issues/19576), since
it had only ever been an implementation detail, and the upgrade guide says the same thing about
the new default. Code written against 1.x could rely on an order Polars never promised, and 2.0
is the first release whose default engine stops providing it.

## The fix is one argument

```{python fix}
import time

def first_q(join_order=None, expr=pl.col("amount").first()):
    if join_order:
        j = ev.join(cu, on="customer_id", how="left", maintain_order=join_order)
    else:
        j = ev.join(cu, on="customer_id", how="left")
    return j.group_by("customer_id").agg(expr).sort("customer_id")

ref = truth["first purchase per customer"]
variants = {
    "default": lambda: first_q().collect(),
    "join(maintain_order='left')": lambda: first_q("left").collect(),
    "sort_by inside the expression":
        lambda: first_q(expr=pl.col("amount").sort_by("event_id").first()).collect(),
    "collect(engine='in-memory')": lambda: first_q().collect(engine="in-memory"),
}
plan = [k for k in variants for _ in range(20)]
np.random.default_rng(7).shuffle(plan)           # interleave, so timing is fair
secs = {k: [] for k in variants}
wrong = {k: 0 for k in variants}
most = {k: 0 for k in variants}
for k in plan:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    out = variants[k]()
    secs[k].append(time.perf_counter() - t0)
    wrong[k] += int(not out.equals(ref))
    most[k] = max(most[k], int((out["amount"] != ref["amount"]).sum()))
for k in variants:
    print(f"{k:31s} wrong {wrong[k]:>2}/20   worst run {most[k]:>2} customers   "
          f"median {np.median(secs[k]):.3f} s")
```

```{r fix-r, include=FALSE}
fx_wrong <- unlist(reticulate::py$wrong)
fx_most <- unlist(reticulate::py$most)
fx_secs <- vapply(reticulate::py$secs, function(s) median(unlist(s)), 1)
mo <- "join(maintain_order='left')"
sb <- "sort_by inside the expression"
im <- "collect(engine='in-memory')"
speed_ratio <- fx_secs[[mo]] / fx_secs[["default"]]
speed_phrase <- if (speed_ratio < 0.9) "ran faster than" else if (speed_ratio > 1.1) "ran slower than" else "ran about as fast as"
stopifnot(fx_wrong[[mo]] == 0, fx_wrong[[sb]] == 0, fx_wrong[[im]] > 0)   # summary relies on these
```

Asking for order worked. Keeping the left table's order in the join and putting `sort_by()` inside
the expression both returned the right answer on all 20 runs. The join fix `r speed_phrase`
the default here (median `r sprintf("%.3f", fx_secs[[mo]])` against
`r sprintf("%.3f", fx_secs[["default"]])` seconds)`r if (speed_ratio <= 1.1) ", so on this data it costs nothing" else ""`.
`sort_by()` is the more robust of the two, because the answer no longer depends on any upstream
step keeping order.

Going back to the old engine `r if (fx_wrong[[im]] == 0) "also worked" else "was not enough"`.
The upgrade guide offers `collect(engine="in-memory")` to restore the previous default, and it
does restore the engine. `r if (fx_wrong[[im]] > 0) paste0("It did not restore the order: on a Parquet source, ", fx_wrong[[im]], " of the 20 runs still came back wrong, by at most ", fx_most[[im]], if (fx_most[[im]] == 1) " customer" else " customers", ". Neither engine promises order, so the fixes that hold are the ones that ask for it.") else ""`
One more caution from the tracker: an optimizer bug that dropped `maintain_order=True` when a
`head()` sat between a group-by and a sort
([issue 30079](https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/issues/30079)) is fixed in 2.1.0, so upgrade
before relying on `maintain_order=True` in that pattern.

## Will your tests catch it?

```{python tests}
from polars.testing import assert_frame_equal

bad = first_q().collect()
print("same shape:", bad.shape == ref.shape, "  same schema:", bad.schema == ref.schema)
try:
    assert_frame_equal(bad, ref, check_row_order=False)
except AssertionError as err:
    print(str(err).splitlines()[0])
```

A test that compares output with a stored answer will catch it, even one that ignores row
order, because the values themselves differ. A test that checks shape, schema, or column names
will pass.

## R users are in the same position

data.table works through rows in the order it holds them, so `amount[1L]` by customer is the
first purchase. DuckDB, which runs in parallel like the streaming engine,
[documents](https://duckdb.org/docs/2.0/sql/functions/aggregates.html) that `first()` can be
non-deterministic without an `ORDER BY`. Same file, same question:

```{r r-engines}
library(data.table)
library(DBI)
ev <- as.data.table(events)
truth_r <- ev[order(event_id), .(amount = amount[1L]), by = customer_id][order(customer_id)]

con <- dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb())
duck <- function(agg) dbGetQuery(con, sprintf(
  "SELECT customer_id, %s AS amount
   FROM read_parquet('%s') e LEFT JOIN read_parquet('%s') c USING (customer_id)
   GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY customer_id",
  agg, normalizePath(events_path, "/"), normalizePath(customers_path, "/")))$amount

engines <- list(
  "data.table, amount[1L]" = function()
    as.data.table(customers)[ev, on = "customer_id"][
      , .(amount = amount[1L]), by = customer_id][order(customer_id)]$amount,
  "DuckDB, first(amount)" = function() duck("first(amount)"),
  "DuckDB, first(amount ORDER BY event_id)" = function() duck("first(amount ORDER BY event_id)"))
r_res <- t(sapply(engines, function(f) {
  bad <- replicate(20, sum(f() != truth_r$amount))
  c(runs_wrong = sum(bad > 0), most_customers_wrong = max(bad))
}))
dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)
r_res
```

```{r r-engines-check, include=FALSE}
stopifnot(r_res[1, "runs_wrong"] == 0, r_res[3, "runs_wrong"] == 0, r_res[2, "runs_wrong"] > 0)
duck_bad <- r_res[2, "runs_wrong"]
```

DuckDB without an `ORDER BY` was wrong on `r duck_bad` of 20 runs, and with one it was right on
all of them. The rule is the same in every parallel engine: if the answer depends on order, say
so in the query.

## What this does not show

- The data are a synthetic event log on one machine with 16 threads. How many rows go wrong
  depends on the thread count and on how the engine splits the work.
- Polars 1.44.2 being right on every run shows what it did, not what it promised.
- `head(20)` was right here. Nothing guarantees that either.

## What to do on Monday

1. Search lazy pipelines for `first()`, `last()`, `cum_sum()`, `unique(keep=...)`,
   `with_row_index()`, and `head()` downstream of a join or a group-by.
2. Add `maintain_order="left"` to the join that feeds them, or put `sort_by()` inside the
   expression.
3. Do not count on `engine="in-memory"` to bring the old order back.
4. Keep one test that compares output with a stored answer. `check_row_order=False` is fine.
5. In SQL, write `first(x ORDER BY t)` or `arg_min(x, t)`.

Whether someone else can rerun your pipeline and get your numbers is the replication standard,
covered in
[A Guide on Data Analysis](https://mike-data-analysis.share.connect.posit.cloud/replication-and-synthetic-data.html).
The two scripts used here, [audit.py](audit.py) and [run_audit.py](run_audit.py), sit next to
this post.
